questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: Where An Instance Name Wins
questions.learningObjective: trace where a name is found when an object and two classes carry it
questions.stem:
A class, a subclass and one object all carry a name with the same spelling, and the object sets its own. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

class Base:
    kind = "base"

class Sub(Base):
    kind = "sub"

    def __init__(self):
        self.own = 1

s = Sub()
s.kind = "own"
print(s.kind, Sub.kind, Base.kind)
print("kind" in s.__dict__, "own" in s.__dict__)

options.text: The name reads as own on the object, sub on the class and base on the parent, and both names are in the instance table, because the object is consulted before either class
The name reads as sub on the object and as sub on both classes with the parent never consulted, because a value in the subclass is taken to hide the one in the parent entirely
options.misconception: believes a class attribute shadow hides the parent value entirely

options.text: The name reads as own on the object and sub on the class, and only the own name is in the instance table, because the kind written on the object replaces the class name rather than joining it
options.misconception: believes writing a name on the object removes it from the class

options.text: The name reads as own on the object and base on the class, and both names are in the instance table, because the search skips the class that defined the name
options.misconception: believes the search skips the class the name came from

questions.explanation: A read of a name on an object looks in the object own table first, then on the class the object was made from, and only then on that class parents in order. Writing a name on the object puts it in the object table without touching the class, which is why the object reports its own value while the class still reports the one the class body wrote. The parent is never skipped: it simply comes later in the order, so it is only consulted when neither the object nor the class has the name. The class table and the object table are separate maps and a write to one is invisible to the other.
questions.hint: Ask which of the three places holding the name is consulted first, and whether writing on the object touches the class.

questions.topic: Which Hook Runs Only After The Search Fails
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the hook that runs for every read from the one that runs only on failure

options.text: The hook reports the same name twice because it remembers the names it has already answered, so the second read is refused and the fallback appears, and the table is still empty
options.misconception: believes the late hook remembers the names it has answered

options.text: The late hook runs for both reads because neither name is in the table, the fallback is never used because the hook answered, and the table is still empty, while the early hook would have run for every read
The late hook runs for both reads and the fallback is used for the second one as well, because the fallback takes over whenever the hook was reached
options.misconception: believes a lookup with a fallback is applied to a name the hook answered

options.text: The hook answers the underscored name and refuses the other, so the fallback appears for the second read, and the table is still empty, because a hook that answers some names is believed to answer only those
options.misconception: believes the late hook only answers names that begin with an underscore

questions.explanation: There are two hooks and they are reached at different moments. The early one is called for every single read, whatever the outcome, and it is the hook that lets a class intercept even names that do exist. The late one is called only after the ordinary search has come back empty, which is why it fired for both reads here and why the fallback never came into play: the hook answered, so there was no failure left to catch. Neither hook writes anything into the object table, so the membership test is still false, and a hook that remembered the names it had answered would stop behaving like a hook and start behaving like a cache.
questions.hint: Ask whether the hook is reached before or after the ordinary search, and whether anything was written.

questions.topic: A Hook That Answers Unknown Names
questions.learningObjective: read a late hook that answers some names and refuses others

options.misconception: believes a refusal stops the hook from being asked again

options.text: The hook reports xa and answers it, then reports zz and answers it, then reports q and the fallback is used anyway, because a fallback is applied even when the read succeeded
options.misconception: believes a fallback applies even to a successful read

options.text: The hook reports xa and answers it in upper case, then reports zz and raises for it, then reports q and the caller falls back because the hook raised, because a fallback catches what the hook refuses
The hook reports xa and answers it in upper case, then reports zz and answers it in upper case as well, then reports q and answers it, because a hook that answers once answers everything
options.misconception: believes a hook that answers one name answers every name

questions.explanation: A late hook is a last chance, and refusing a name from it is exactly the same as the name not existing at all, so the failure surfaces to whoever asked. That is what makes a hook able to hide names from most of a program while the rest of the program carries on, and it is also the trap: a hook that returns something for a name it should refuse will quietly invent attributes that no code can enumerate. A fallback is applied when the read fails, not when it succeeds, so the third line reports the fallback only because the hook refused. Nothing is written into the table by any of this.
questions.hint: Ask what a refusal from the hook is equivalent to, and when a fallback is applied.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: A Hook That Answers Everything
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a hook that never refuses, so a fallback can never fire
questions.stem:
A class answers every unknown name with a fixed value, so a lookup with a fallback is expected to be protected. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What goes wrong, and what does it actually print?

class G:
    def __getattr__(self, name):
        return None

g = G()
print(g.anything)
print(getattr(g, "missing", "fallback"))
print("a" in g.__dict__)

options.text: The hook answers the first read and the second reports the fallback, because a lookup with a fallback is applied whenever the name is not in the table
options.misconception: believes a fallback is applied to any name absent from the table

options.text: The hook answers the first read and the second reports the fallback, and the table gains the name afterwards, because asking for a name is believed to put it there
options.misconception: believes asking for a name inserts it into the table

options.text: The first read raises and the run stops, because returning a fixed value is believed to be rejected as not a real answer
options.misconception: believes a fixed value is rejected by a lookup

options.text: The hook answers for every name, so both reads report the fixed value and the fallback never appears, and the table is still empty, because a hook that always answers makes the object claim to hold every name

questions.explanation: A lookup with a fallback is a request that says give me this name or give me that value instead, and it can only use the second half of the bargain when the first half fails. A hook that answers every name means the first half never fails, so the fallback is unreachable and the object appears to hold every name anyone asks for. That is the harder kind of bug to find later, because nothing raises and nothing is written, and the symptom shows up far from the cause as a value that should have been a name. The fix is to make the hook raise for names it does not recognise, which restores the failure that the rest of the program is written to expect.
questions.hint: Ask whether the first half of a lookup with a fallback can ever fail when the hook always answers.

questions.topic: A Missing Name With A Fallback
questions.learningObjective: read a lookup with a fallback against a name that really exists
questions.stem:
A class carries one real name, and a lookup with a fallback is made first for a name that exists and then for one that does not. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

class R:
    v = 1

r = R()
print(getattr(r, "v", "fallback"), getattr(r, "w", "fallback"))
r.w = 2
print(getattr(r, "w", "fallback"))
print(sorted(r.__dict__))

options.text: The existing name reports its real value and the missing one reports the fallback, then after the name is written it reports its own value, and the object table holds the one name that was written on it while the other stays a class value
Both reads report the fallback, because a lookup with a fallback is applied whether or not the name exists, and the table then holds the name that was written on it with a value of 2 in it
options.misconception: believes a fallback replaces a real value as well

options.text: The existing name reports the fallback and the missing one reports the fallback, because a value held on the class is not taken to be a real value, and the table then holds the one name that was written on it
options.misconception: believes a value held on the class does not count as existing

options.text: The existing name reports its real value, the missing one reports the fallback, and after the name is written the read still reports 2 because the table is taken to be read once and remembered, and the table holds that name
options.misconception: believes the object table is read once and then remembered

questions.explanation: A lookup with a fallback asks the object first and uses the second value only if the object cannot supply the name, so a name the class carries counts as supplied and the first read reports the real value. Once the name is written on the object it becomes a real name of the object in its own right, and the second read of it reports that value rather than the fallback. The printed table holds only the name that was written on the object, because the other one lives on the class and the two tables are kept apart, which is also why writing on the object cannot be seen to change anything about the class.
questions.hint: Ask whether the fallback is used when the object can supply the name at all.

questions.topic: Why A Data Descriptor Wins Over The Instance Table
questions.learningObjective: say which of two kinds of class attribute takes precedence over the object table

options.text: The object table wins against the first and against the second, so the first read reports the written value and after the write the read reports mine as well, and the last line reports True then False
options.misconception: believes the class value disappears once the object stores its own

options.text: The write on the object wins against the class attribute that only defines a read, the write against the class attribute that also defines a write is refused, and the last line is the test that separates them
Both class attributes win against the object table, so the class reports the read hook answer and the object reports the written value, and the second write is refused as well
options.misconception: believes every class attribute outranks the object table

options.text: The object table wins against both, so the first read reports the written value and the second write stores its value and the read then reports that stored value
options.misconception: believes the object table always wins

questions.explanation: The dividing line is whether the class attribute defines a write hook as well as a read hook, and that is exactly what the last line tests. An attribute that only reads sits below the object table, so a write on the object is found first on the way back and the class value is left alone; the read still goes through the class because nothing in the object table shadows it any more. An attribute that also writes sits above the object table, so the write is handed to the class, and a class that refuses produces an error rather than a stored value. That is how a read-only value is built, and it is why the two look similar in the class body and behave in opposite ways at run time.
questions.hint: Ask whether the class attribute defines a write hook, and where the object table sits relative to it.

The read-only class attribute answers both reads and the object table still holds the written value, because a class attribute is always consulted before the object table

The distinction that matters in review is between refusing and storing, because a hook that stores and then refuses looks identical from the outside and leaves the object in a state nobody asked for.

questions.topic: A Function In A Class Body Takes Its First Argument
questions.learningObjective: read a plain function used as a class attribute and the object it receives
questions.stem:
A plain function is placed in a class body and then reached through the class and through an object. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

def m(self):
    return self.k

class M:
    fn = m

mm = M()
mm.k = 7
print(mm.fn(), M.fn(mm), M.fn is m)
print(callable(M.fn), callable(mm.fn))

options.text: The call through the class reports the value and the call through the object stops with a TypeError about a required positional argument, and the class attribute reports itself under a different name, because the class body turned the function into a value that takes no object
options.misconception: believes the class body changed the function into a value that takes no object

options.text: Both calls report the value, the class attribute is the same function object, and the bound method reports the plain function name because binding is believed to rename it
options.misconception: believes binding renames the function it came from

options.text: Both calls report the value stored on the object, the class attribute is the same function object, and both the plain function and the bound method report as callable

The call through the object reports the value and the call through the class stops with a TypeError saying a required positional argument is missing, because the function is not given an object to read from
options.misconception: believes a class access cannot reach the function at all

questions.explanation: A function is a descriptor, which is why putting one in a class body does not turn it into an ordinary method by magic: the machinery notices the function and passes the object as its first argument when it is reached through an instance. The same function reached through the class gets no object, so it has to be handed one explicitly, and that is the difference between the two calls in the first line. The class body stores the function object itself rather than a copy, and both the plain function and the bound method report as callable because binding only supplies an argument.
questions.hint: Ask what a function receives when it is reached through an object rather than through its class.

A lazy value counts how many times its body ran across two objects, and the shape of the cached form is checked. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

import functools

class Box:
    made = 0

    @functools.cached_property
    def value(self):
        Box.made += 1
        return Box.made

a, b = Box(), Box()
print(a.value, b.value, a.value)
print(Box.made)
print(hasattr(functools.cached_property, "__get__"), hasattr(functools.cached_property, "__set__"))
print("value" in a.__dict__, "value" in Box.__dict__)

options.misconception: believes the cached form defines a write hook

options.text: The first object gets 1, the second gets 2, and reading the first again still gives 1, so the body ran twice across two objects, and the cached form has a read hook but no write hook, with the stored value on the object and the attribute itself still in the class table
The first object gets 1 and the second also gets 1, so the body ran once across two objects, and the stored value is believed to sit on the class rather than on each object
options.misconception: believes the cached value is held on the class

options.text: The first object gets 1, the second gets 2, and reading the first again still gives 1, and the last line is believed to report False because the attribute itself is taken to sit on the object rather than in the class table
options.misconception: believes the attribute itself is not in the class table

The counter is a class figure and counts the two runs across both objects, so it agrees with the two distinct values that came out. The last two lines are the mechanism rather than the symptom: the form defines a read hook and no write hook, and the value turns up on the object and not on the class, which is exactly what lets the object table shadow it on the next read.

A lazy value is read, then written over by a plain assignment, then read again, and the shape of the form is checked. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. Which statement about what happened is correct?

class Box:
    @functools.cached_property
    def value(self):
        return 1

b = Box()
print(b.value, "value" in b.__dict__)
b.value = 9
print(b.value, "value" in b.__dict__)
print(hasattr(functools.cached_property, "__set__"))

options.text: The first read stores the value, the assignment is believed to be refused because the name is already taken by the class, and the second read still reports the stored value
options.misconception: believes a cached name refuses assignment

options.text: The first read stores the value, the assignment overwrites it, the second read reports what was assigned, and the body is believed to have run twice so the call count reaches two
options.misconception: believes an assignment clears the cached entry

options.text: The first read stores the value, the assignment overwrites that stored entry rather than running the body, the second read reports what was assigned, and the write hook is absent, which is why the object table was reachable
The first read stores the value and the second read reports what was assigned rather than the body output, because an assignment is believed to run the cached body again
options.misconception: believes an assignment runs the cached body

questions.hint: Ask whether a write hook exists, and therefore whether the write reaches the class or the object table.

questions.learningObjective: read a metaclass hook that reports every construction of a class

options.text: The hook reports the class name and the arguments before the object exists, the object then reports the value it stored, and the type of the class is the metaclass that was named
The hook reports the class name and the stored value of the object after it exists, so the value is available inside the hook, and the type of the class is the metaclass that was named

options.text: The hook is never reached because a class using a metaclass cannot be called, and the program stops at the class statement

options.text: The hook reports once when the class was declared rather than on each use, so the line appears before the class statement finishes
options.misconception: believes the hook fires once at class creation

The type of the class is the metaclass that was named, which the last line confirms, and that is the relationship the whole mechanism rests on: a class is an object whose type is chosen when the class statement runs.

questions.topic: Two Construction Hooks In Order
questions.learningObjective: read the order of the two hooks that build an object
questions.stem:
A class defines both construction hooks, each reports what it was given, and one object is made. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

class P3:
    def __new__(cls, v):
        print("new", v)
        obj = super().__new__(cls)
        obj.made = v
        return obj

    def __init__(self, v):
        print("init", v)
        self.v = v

q = P3(4)
print(q.made, q.v)

options.text: Only the first hook reports and both figures come out as the argument, because the second hook was left doing nothing at all
options.misconception: believes the second hook is optional and does nothing when it is empty

options.text: Both hooks report for each object in turn and the pair of objects carries the values passed to them, because every construction runs the pair
options.misconception: believes both hooks run once per object made

options.text: The first hook reports before the second and both figures on the object come out as the value that was passed, because the first hook makes the object and the second fills it in
Only the second hook reports, the made name is reported as absent, and the value comes out as the argument, because a class that does not define the first hook has nothing to report for it
options.misconception: believes only the second hook runs when the first is absent

questions.explanation: Constructing an object is two steps and the machinery always takes them in the same sequence. The first hook is asked for a new object and may return anything, including an object of some other class, which is how a class can hand back something it did not create. If it returns an instance of the class being built, the second hook is then called on that object to finish it off. That is why the first hook is where a frozen or an interned value belongs and the second is where ordinary setup belongs, and why a first hook that forgets to return anything produces an object that the second hook then has to cope with.
questions.hint: Ask which hook is asked for the object itself and which is called on the result.

class Adder:
    def __call__(self, n):
        return n + 10

a = Adder()
print(a(5), callable(a), isinstance(a, Adder))
print(a.__call__(5), type(a).__name__)

options.misconception: believes an object cannot be called with brackets

options.text: Calling with brackets gives 15 and the object reports as callable but not as an instance, because being callable replaces being an instance
options.misconception: believes being callable replaces being an instance

options.text: Calling with brackets gives 15 and the object reports as an instance but not as callable, because the class is not a function
options.misconception: believes an instance of a callable class does not report as callable

options.text: Calling with brackets gives 15 and the object reports as both callable and an instance of its class, and calling the hook directly gives the same figure beside the class name

The two tests in the first line answer different questions and both are true here: callable asks whether the object can be called at all, and the instance test asks whether it belongs to a class. Calling the hook directly gives the same figure as calling with brackets, which is the check worth writing when a wrapper around a callable starts producing different answers depending on how it was reached.
questions.hint: Ask which hook the brackets reach, and what each of the two tests in the first line is asking.

A class says what whole number it stands for, and that object is used as a position and as a slice bound. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

class Idx:
    def __index__(self):
        return 3

i = Idx()
print([0, 1, 2, 3, 4][i], "abcdef"[i], "abcdef"[:i])
print(hasattr(Idx, "__index__"), hasattr(Idx, "__int__"))

options.misconception: believes using an object as a position requires a length hook

options.misconception: believes the object itself is used as the position

options.text: The list gives 3, the string gives d, the slice keeps abc, and the class defines the index hook rather than the integer conversion
The list raises a type error about needing integers, the string and slice are not reached, and the class defines the integer conversion rather than the index hook
options.misconception: believes the hook must be the integer conversion

questions.explanation: A position and a slice bound both have to be whole numbers, so the machinery asks the object for a whole number rather than accepting the object itself. That is what the index hook is for, and it is a different hook from the integer conversion: a value that converts to a number is not automatically usable as a position, and the error messages are different. Using the same object for a list index, a string index and a slice bound works precisely because all three ask the same question, which makes it a convenient way to express a position once and use it in several places.

A class reports the specification it is handed rather than a value, and the same class is used inside a field, as a bare format and as a direct call. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

class Money:
    def __format__(self, spec):
        return f"[{spec}]"

m = Money()
print(f"{m:>10}|", format(m, "abc"))
print(format(m), format(m, ""))
print(len(format(m, ">10")))

options.misconception: believes the field is applied again to the returned text

options.text: The field hands over the specification, a bare format reports the word none because no specification was given, and the same specification produces a string of length five
options.misconception: believes a bare format is given a substitute specification

options.text: The field hands over the specification and gets it back inside brackets, a bare format reports empty brackets, and the same specification produces a string of length five

options.misconception: believes a bare format falls back to the text form

That is why a class that reports the specification instead of a value can be placed inside a field and still come out exactly the length the caller asked for: the hook is responsible for the width, not the machinery. A bare format is not a special case, it is the same call with an empty specification, which is what the middle line shows and what makes the length on the last line predictable.

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

c = Node("c")
a.peer = c
c.peer = a

That is why the third line reports the object as gone only after the collection call, and why the difference between the second and third lines is the whole point of the pair.

questions.topic: What Holds A Generator Between Two Reads
questions.learningObjective: explain what keeps a partly read generator alive
questions.stem:
A generator yields once, takes a value back, and yields again, and the object is inspected before and after it is exhausted. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does that tell you about what is held between two reads?

def gen(n):
    x = yield n
    yield x * 2

g = gen(3)
print(type(g).__name__)
print(g.gi_code.co_name, g.gi_frame.f_code.co_name)
print(next(g))
print(g.send(5))
print(g.gi_frame is None)

answer.exemplar: Calling a function that contains a yield does not run the body; it makes a generator object, and the body has not started yet. The first read runs the body up to the first yield and then leaves it suspended, which is why the object reports a code object and a frame that both belong to the function that made it. Everything the body had computed is still in that frame, which is what makes the second read resume rather than restart, and why a value sent into the generator arrives as the result of the yield expression. The frame is released only when the body runs off the end or is closed, so an exhausted generator reports no frame at all while a suspended one keeps its locals alive for as long as the object exists. That is also why a generator that yields inside a loop over a large structure holds a reference to that structure for as long as the reader takes to finish with it.

questions.explanation: A generator is a suspended call. Its frame stays alive between reads, holding the local names the body had, and the next read continues from the yield rather than starting again, which is the whole difference between a generator and a function called in a loop. The frame is released when the body finishes or the object is closed, and until then the generator is keeping whatever those names refer to, so a generator that yields from inside a large structure extends that structure lifetime for as long as the reader is slow.

questions.topic: Why A Default Is Evaluated Once
questions.learningObjective: read a default that is shared between every call
questions.stem:
A function takes a list as its default and appends to it, three calls are made with no argument, and the default is then reported on. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

def f(box=[]):
    box.append(1)
    return len(box)

print(f(), f(), f())
print(f.__defaults__)
print(len(f.__defaults__[0]))
print(f.__defaults__[0])

options.text: Each call gives 1, the default is a one-entry tuple holding an empty list, that list still holds nothing, and it is still there after the calls, because a mutable default is taken to be copied before it is handed over
options.misconception: believes a mutable default is copied for each call

options.text: The three calls give 1, then 2, then 3, the default is a one-entry tuple holding a list of three ones, and the list is the same object every call would see, because the name is taken to be shared with the module as well
options.misconception: believes the default is shared with the module

options.text: The three calls give 1, then 2, then 3, the default is a one-entry tuple holding a list of three ones, and the list is the same object every call would see

Each call gives 1, the default is a one-entry tuple holding nothing at all, that entry is not reported as missing, and the short name of the function is f, because a default is taken to be written out at the call
options.misconception: believes a default is written out at each call

questions.explanation: A default is written once, when the definition runs, and the object it names is then the default for every call that does not pass one. With a mutable object that means the state accumulates across calls, which is the bug behind a surprising number of reports of a function that remembers. The fix is a default of nothing at all, with the real value built inside the call, so the object is made fresh each time and no two calls share anything.

questions.topic: What A First Assignment Does To A Class Attribute
questions.learningObjective: explain what assigning to a class attribute on an object changes
questions.stem:
A class carries a name, two objects are made and both read it, one of them is written to and then the write is undone, and the tables are inspected. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. Which statement about the write is correct?

class C:
    size = 1

a, b = C(), C()
print(C.size, a.size, b.size)
a.size = 5
print(C.size, a.size, b.size)
del a.size
print(C.size, a.size)
print(sorted(k for k in vars(a) if not k.startswith("__")))
print("size" in vars(C), "size" in vars(a))

options.text: All of them read 1 at first, after the class is written the class reads 5 and so do both objects, the object table is empty, and the name is in the class table and not in the object table
options.misconception: believes writing on an object writes the class name

options.text: All of them read 1 at first, after the write the class reads 1, the object that was written reads 5 and the other still reads 1, after the write is undone all of them read 1 again, the object table is empty, and the name is in the class table and not in the other object table
options.misconception: believes the write is shared by every object

options.text: All of them read 1 at first, after the write and the undo all of them read 1 again, the object table is empty, the name is in the class table and not in the object table, and the class name multiplied by ten gives ten
options.misconception: believes the undo removes the class name

options.text: All of them read 1 at first, after the write the class still reads 1 while the object that was written reads 5 and the other still reads 1, after the write is undone both read 1 again, the object table is empty, and the name is in the class table and not in the object table

questions.explanation: A read of a name on an object looks in the object first and then at the class, but a write only ever touches the object, so the first assignment to a name that came from the class creates a private copy and leaves the class alone. Reading the name again then finds the private copy, and another object of the same class is unaffected, which is exactly the behaviour that makes a configurable default on a class quietly stop being a default. Undoing the write removes the private copy and the class value shows through again, so a class-level default can be restored without touching the class.
questions.hint: Ask where a write goes and what it leaves behind, and what undoing it removes.
